faq.a1: Fill in the request form on the relevant company page (Daryadaran Tous for transport, Harmoniza Hormoz Arian for terminal, Hami Hamrah Jonoub for bulk, Naghel Al-Aswad for trade), call 09153143647, or leave a message in the live chat. We reply within 24 business hours.
faq.a10: Rates are quoted based on cargo type, weight/volume, route, equipment type (wagon, container, truck), season, port/terminal charges and Incoterms. The formal proforma invoice includes all cost items and becomes binding once you confirm it.
faq.a2: Identity or company details (national ID or registration number), contact information, origin and destination, cargo type and weight, Incoterms, and a packing list and proforma invoice if available. For special cargoes, technical and insurance documents are also requested.
faq.a3: Yes. Cargo insurance can be arranged under standard Institute Cargo Clauses (ICC A, B or C) for the value of the goods (CIF/CFR + 10%), and its conditions are included in the contract before execution. We recommend full-value cover for high-value shipments.
faq.a4: Yes. A dedicated specialist is assigned to every file, and the cargo status (loading, border crossing, terminal entry, unloading, delivery) is reported regularly by SMS, email or messenger.
faq.a5: Depending on the cooperation model: advance payment on order, documentary credit (L/C) or telegraphic transfer (T/T) for foreign trade, and staged invoicing for logistics projects. Details are stated in the formal proforma invoice.
faq.a6: Incoterms are the international standard defining seller and buyer responsibilities in delivery. The right choice depends on the route, mode of transport and how much control you want over the supply chain; the full guide is in the Incoterms 2020 chapter, and our specialist can recommend the best option for your cargo.
faq.a7: Yes, in compliance with IMDG (sea), ADR/RID (road/rail) regulations and using suitable equipment (reefer containers, insulated wagons). Safety Data Sheets (MSDS) and cargo classification are reviewed before acceptance.
faq.a8: Yes. The “Chat with a specialist” button is active on every page; during working hours you get an online reply, and outside working hours you can leave a message and your contact details so we can call you back. Every chat message is also emailed to the specialist.
faq.a9: Our main corridors include Iraq, Pakistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates and Afghanistan, plus shipping lines from China and rail transport from the CIS region. For details on each route, visit the Affiliated Companies page.

c1.h3b: Four legal pillars of international trade
c1.o1: Negotiation and agreement on price, delivery terms and Incoterms
c1.o2: Conclusion of the sales contract with cargo description, quality, packaging and delivery time
c1.o3: Payment arrangement (advance payment, L/C or T/T)
c1.o5: Transport, insurance and preparation of shipping documents
c1.o6: Customs clearance at origin and destination
c1.o7: Cargo delivery, final settlement and file closure
c1.p1: International trade is the exchange of goods and services between parties from different legal, monetary and customs systems. Unlike domestic trade, these deals carry extra risks: exchange-rate fluctuations, differing laws, transport distance, risk of damage in transit, sanctions and documentary requirements.
c1.u1: International sales contract: applicable domestic law or the CISG (United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods, 1980) as the parties agree.
c1.u2: Incoterms: define delivery, cost and risk allocation between seller and buyer.
c1.u3: Transport and payment documents: bill of lading, CMR, letter of credit, etc.
c1.u4: General regulations: customs, sanctions, insurance and competition/export-control law.

c10.p1: Persian and English equivalents of the most common international trade and transport terms:

c2.h3a: Terms suited to each mode of transport
c2.p1: Incoterms are the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) standard that, through eleven terms, draw the line of seller and buyer responsibility for delivery, cost allocation and transfer of risk. The current edition is Incoterms 2020 and, like previous editions, it is not contractually binding — it only applies when referenced in the contract.
c2.u1: State costs in alphabetical order in the contract document to avoid ambiguity.
c2.u2: Under FCA the seller may obtain an Onboard bill of lading so they can use a letter of credit.
c2.u3: CIF/CIP set a minimum insurance cover; for high-value cargo agree ICC (A) cover.
c2.u4: For multimodal shipments, EXW and FOB are higher-risk choices; FCA or CPT/CIP are usually more suitable.
c2.u5: Incoterms do not by themselves transfer title, validate the contract or override customs requirements.

c3.notice: Customs regulations are amended frequently; always confirm tariff codes, duties and mandatory permits with the Islamic Republic of Iran Customs Administration and a licensed consultant.
c3.o1: Register the order and obtain permits before the goods arrive
c3.o2: Declare the goods to customs (e-declaration and the Single Window for cross-border trade)
c3.o3: Valuation, duty assessment and mandatory standards
c3.o4: Clearance or transfer to a bonded warehouse
c3.o5: Visit the bank/exchange office for currency transfer per regulations
c3.p1: Every goods crossing a border is subject to that country's tariff, technical regulations and special requirements. The World Customs Organization's Harmonized System (HS) is the common language of goods description: each product has a ten-digit national tariff code and a six-digit international code.
c3.u1: Commercial invoice with cargo description, value and sales terms
c3.u2: Packing list with net/gross weight and number of packages
c3.u3: Bill of lading or other transport document suited to the mode
c3.u4: Cargo insurance policy (under CIF/CIP terms or as requested)
c3.u5: Certificates of origin, health, inspection or standards as required by cargo type
c3.u6: Customs declaration and special permits (Health, Agriculture, Standards organizations, etc.)

c4.h3a: Letter of Credit (L/C) — the heart of documentary trade
c4.p1: In international trade, money replaces trust. The three main payment methods are advance payment, bank transfer (T/T) and the Letter of Credit; Documentary Collection is a middle path.
c4.p1a: A letter of credit is an unconditional undertaking by the issuing bank that guarantees payment when conforming documents are presented. The most important rule is the credit's independence from the underlying contract: the bank looks only at the documents, not the goods.
c4.p2: The most common practical method; usually a combination of advance payment (30–50%) and settlement after document copies are sent or goods are delivered. For a first deal with a new counterparty, safeguards such as a letter of credit or staged sampling are recommended.
c4.t: Letters of credit, payment and collection
c4.u1: Types: revocable (rare today), irrevocable, confirmed and standby letters of credit.
c4.u2: Key rule: an L/C is governed by UCP 600 if it says so.
c4.u3: Typical documents: bill of lading, invoice, packing list, certificate of origin, inspection certificate and insurance policy.
c4.u4: Compliance: documents must strictly match the credit's terms; even minor differences can cause a discrepancy and extra cost.
c4.u5: D/P (Documents against Payment): documents are released to the buyer only after payment.
c4.u6: D/A (Documents against Acceptance): documents are released against the buyer's written undertaking to pay at maturity.
c4.u7: These methods are cheaper than an L/C but carry no bank payment guarantee and are governed by URC 522.

c5.p1: A transport document is the receipt for goods with the carrier, the start of the carriage obligation and in some cases the instrument of title transfer. Each mode of transport has its own document and rules.
c5.t: Transport documents: CMR, bill of lading, AWB and CIM/SMGS
c5.u1: In a sea bill of lading, a “Clean B/L” means the goods were received apparently in good order; a claused remark can disrupt a letter of credit.
c5.u2: Multimodal shipments use combined transport documents.
c5.u3: The time limit for damage claims under the CMR road convention is usually 21 days after delivery (see the relevant rule for details).
c5.u4: Keeping document copies and aligning the consignee name across documents and contracts matters greatly.

c6.notice: Warning: this chapter is a general educational overview only, not a legal interpretation or official opinion. For any customs case, use a customs legal advisor and the official authorities (Islamic Republic of Iran Customs Administration, Trade Promotion Organization).
c6.p1: Iran's customs framework rests on the Customs Affairs Law, import/export regulations and the national tariff (ten-digit HS). Goods fall into four general groups:
c6.p2: The final rate of each good is calculated from the customs base value, tariff, national duties, taxes and possibly VAT, and is affected by annual approvals and tariff sanctions.
c6.u1: Group 1 (basic goods): eligible for preferential exchange rates and duty discounts.
c6.u2: Group 2: customs duties below the full rate.
c6.u5: Single Window for cross-border trade to integrate permits
c6.u7: Standards, health and sectoral permit systems (National Permits Gateway)
c6.u8: Free zones and special economic areas with duty exemptions or discounts

c7.notice: This chapter is a general overview; every transaction's sanctions assessment must be performed by a sanctions-law specialist.
c7.o1: Know your counterparty: verify name, beneficial owners and country of interest (KYC) against sanctions lists.
c7.o2: Know the cargo: HS code and possible dual-use or military application.
c7.o3: Know the route: the port, shipping line, bank and financial intermediaries involved.
c7.o4: Record and archive: keep transaction documents at least for the statutory retention period.
c7.o5: Training and periodic review: keep lists and processes up to date.
c7.p1: International sanctions are economic restrictions imposed by the UN Security Council, the European Union, the United States (OFAC) and other bodies. For every international trade practitioner, a Compliance Program is a practical necessity, not a formality.
c7.u1: Terms such as “final destination” or “end-user” in documents must match reality.
c7.u2: Payments should flow through transparent, traceable banking channels.
c7.u3: At the slightest doubt, suspend the deal and consult legal counsel.
c7.u4: Sanctions rules are not static and can change overnight; continuous updating is essential.

c8.h3a: Key points of the insurance contract
c8.p1: Cargo Insurance covers loss arising from marine, road, rail and air incidents. The most widely used terms are the Institute Cargo Clauses (ICC), offered at three levels:
c8.u1: ICC (A): near-all-risks cover except expressly excluded perils; the default under CIP.
c8.u2: ICC (B): cover for loss caused by named perils such as fire, explosion, overturning, collision and sea water.
c8.u3: ICC (C): minimum cover; major losses such as sinking, fire or overturning; the default under CIF.
c8.u4: Insured value: usually CIF value plus 10% (CIF + 10%) to cover expected profit.
c8.u5: Additional covers: War and Strikes clauses are usually added separately.
c8.u6: Voyage and Time insurance: the first for a single voyage, the second for a defined period.
c8.u7: Claims procedure: immediate notice of loss, preparation of documents (customary protest, bill of lading, invoice) and the insurer's right of subrogation.
c8.u8: Carrier liability and General Average: in cases of voluntary sacrifice (such as jettisoning cargo at sea), all stakeholders share the loss.

c9.p1: International commercial disputes are usually settled by arbitration rather than national courts, because arbitral awards are recognizable and enforceable in more than 170 states party to the 1958 New York Convention.
c9.u1: Specify the seat of arbitration; the seat determines the procedural law governing the process.
c9.u2: State the number of arbitrators (usually one or three), the language and the applicable rules.
c9.u3: Choose an enforceable governing law, such as Iranian law, English law or the CISG.
c9.u4: An initial good-faith attempt to settle amicably is common and useful.

geo.desc: The Sarakhs Free Trade-Industrial Zone lies about 150 km east of Mashhad, adjacent to the Iran–Turkmenistan border. Having started operations in the 1990s and upgraded to free-zone status through 1402 (2023) approvals and 1403 (2024) regulations, the zone covers about 5,290 hectares and is the main hub of Iranian trade with Turkmenistan and Central Asian countries. Estimates show that the bulk of Iran's rail transit passes through the Sarakhs border.
